questions.q: Meera's project note reads: 'The Rai stones of Yap Island were giant discs of rock. Being too heavy to carry about, they cannot have been money.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the Rai stones were used as money on Yap Island, so being heavy does not stop a thing being money; heaviness only makes it hard to carry. The note wrongly treats the stones as a commodity or as the money of another place.
o: Weight does not decide it; the chapter says the Rai stones were money on Yap Island
She is right, because money in the chapter is always light enough to be carried about from place to place
She is right, because the chapter calls the Rai stones goods that were swapped in barter and never used as money
She is wrong, because the Rai stones were used as money in Central Mexico and the lands near it

questions.q: True or False: A copper chopping-knife in Central Mexico and a coil of red feathers on the Solomon Islands could both be called money, because what makes a thing money, in the chapter's sense, is that people accept and use it for making or receiving payments, not the material it is made of. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter defines money as the common tool that everybody accepts and uses to make or receive payments, and it shows the Tajadero (copper, Central Mexico and parts of Central America) and the Tevau (bird feathers, Solomon Islands) as forms of money, so the material does not decide it.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: money is defined by being accepted for payments, and the copper Tajadero and feather Tevau were both money

questions.q: A trader's day-book for one day records: (1) 3 kg of millet taken, 1 kg of salt given; (2) a pair of sandals given, ₹90 taken; (3) a day's cart work given, a week's milk taken; (4) 2 kg of tea given, ₹40 taken; (5) a goat given, a plough taken. The number of entries that are barter is ___.

A teacher puts three pictures on the board: a giant disc of rock, a copper chopping knife and a coil of red feathers. She asks which idea of the chapter the three pictures show together. Which answer is best?
questions.a: The three were forms of money used in different places, so very different objects can serve as money where people accept them. The other answers claim a single metal, a single island or a rule about carrying that the chapter does not give.
o: Very different objects served as money in different parts of the world over time
Money has always been made of metal, and these three were early coins that wore away
All three were used on Yap Island, so that island had the widest barter anywhere
Barter works only with objects that are easy to carry from one place to another

questions.q: Rohan swaps his spare eraser for Imran's spare pencil. Later Rohan pays ₹10 at the school shop for another pencil. (a) In the words of the chapter's glossary, in what way are the two deals alike? (b) What single feature makes only the first one barter?
questions.a: (a) Both are transactions, pieces of business done between people. (b) In the first deal no money is used and the goods are exchanged directly, while in the second the ₹10 is the common tool of payment.
s: Part (a): both are transactions, pieces of business between people
Part (b): the first uses no money and swaps goods directly; the second pays in rupees

questions.q:
Read the statements about the barter system and money.
1. The chapter lists cowrie shells, salt, tea, tobacco and cloth among the commodities that people used in barter.
2. The Tajadero, used as money in Central Mexico and parts of Central America, was a coil of red bird feathers.
3. The chapter's glossary describes a transaction as a piece of business between people, especially an act of buying or selling.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: the Tajadero was a copper chopping knife, and the coil of red feathers was the Tevau of the Solomon Islands.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Four neighbours settle their accounts with the tailor without handing over a single coin or note. Which settlement is NOT barter?
questions.a: Scanning a QR code moves digital money, which the chapter describes as money in electronic form, so the payment is not barter even though no coin or note is seen. The other three swap goods or services directly with no money at all.
o: Pooja scans a QR code displayed at the tailor's counter and pays ₹450 for her stitching
Vikram teaches the tailor's son for a month and takes a school shirt for his help
Suma gives the tailor a sack of potatoes and takes a stitched blouse in exchange
Naseem fixes the tailor's door and has his own curtains stitched in return for it

questions.q: Tina says, 'In barter, the two sides must give things of equal price, and no money may pass.' Which part of her statement agrees with the chapter, and which part does not? Explain.
questions.a: She is partly right. 'No money may pass' agrees with the chapter, which defines the barter system as exchanging goods and services without using money. 'Equal price' is not part of that definition; the chapter says people have to settle in what proportion the goods should be exchanged, which is a difficulty, not a rule.
s: Verdict: partly right
Agreeing part: no money is used, as in the glossary definition of the barter system
Other part: equal price is not in the definition; the proportion has to be settled by the two people

questions.q: (a) Name the place and the material of the Rai stones and of the Tevau. (b) Using the chapter's idea of portability, say which of the two would be easier to carry to a distant place, and why.
questions.a: (a) Rai stones: Yap Island, giant discs of rock. Tevau: Solomon Islands, a red coil made from birds' feathers. (b) The Tevau; portability is the ability of an object to be carried from one place to another, and a coil of feathers is far easier to move than a giant rock disc.
s: Part (a): Rai stones, Yap Island, rock; Tevau, Solomon Islands, bird feathers
Part (b): the Tevau, since portability is ease of carrying and giant rock discs are hard to move

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A tailor who stitches a shirt for a farmer and takes a bag of wheat in return is part of a barter system.
Reason (R): Cowrie shells, salt, tea and cloth were among the commodities that people used in barter.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true. The tailor's deal is barter because a service is exchanged for goods without money, which is the chapter's definition; the list of commodities does not explain that, so R is not the explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A school plans a 'no-money' swap fair where children exchange goods and services. Which rule would stop the fair from being barter, by the chapter's meaning?
questions.a: Barter is exchange of goods and services without using money, so letting children buy items for rupees brings money in. The other rules keep every exchange direct, one thing or help for another.
o: Any child may buy an item from the fair's counter by paying ₹5 in cash
A child may offer an hour of homework help in return for a storybook
Two friends may swap their snacks directly without fixing a price
A child may exchange a toy she has outgrown for a game a classmate has finished

questions.q: Describe a real situation from your school or neighbourhood that is barter. Then change one detail so that it is no longer barter, and explain why it stopped being barter.
questions.a: Example: Asha gives her old story book to Rita and takes Rita's colouring set. If Rita pays ₹40 for the book instead, it is a purchase, because money is now the means of payment and the goods are not swapped directly.
s: Gives a situation in which goods or services are swapped without money
Changes one detail, such as adding a payment in rupees
Explains that barter needs the exchange to be direct, without money

questions.q: Fatima says, 'Barter and money are the same thing: in both, people hand over something they have to get something they need.' (a) What does the chapter's definition of money add that barter does not have? (b) Give your own example of a service being exchanged for goods, to show a transaction without money.
questions.a: (a) Money is the common tool that everybody accepts and uses to make or receive payments, whereas barter exchanges goods and services without any such tool. (b) Example: a tutor teaches a neighbour's child for a month and takes a sack of rice, with no money used.
s: Part (a): money is the common tool everybody accepts for payments; barter works without it
Part (b): a correct example of a service swapped for goods without money

questions.q: Gauri makes baskets and wants rice. Hari grows rice and wants someone to teach his son. Isha is a teacher and wants a basket. Nobody in the village uses money. (a) Arrange who gives what to whom so that all three get what they want. (b) Name the goods and the service involved. (c) Why is each of these exchanges a transaction, and why is the whole arrangement barter?
questions.a: (a) Gauri gives a basket to Isha, Isha teaches Hari's son, and Hari gives rice to Gauri, so each receives what she or he wants. (b) The baskets and the rice are goods and the teaching is a service. (c) Each exchange is a piece of business between people, so it is a transaction; all of them swap goods and services directly without any money, which is barter.
s: Part (a): basket from Gauri to Isha, teaching from Isha to Hari's son, rice from Hari to Gauri
Part (b): baskets and rice as goods, teaching as the service
Part (c): each exchange is a piece of business between people, so a transaction
Part (c): no money is used anywhere, so the arrangement is barter

questions.q: Mahesh, a carpenter, makes a cupboard for Lalita and takes 40 kg of rice in return. Lalita says, 'I paid in rice, so rice is money in our village now.' (a) Is the deal barter? Why? (b) Does her conclusion follow from the chapter's definition of money? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Yes, the cupboard and the rice are swapped directly with no money used. (b) No. Money is the common tool that everybody accepts and uses to make or receive payments; one deal paid in rice does not show that everybody in the village accepts rice for payments.
s: Part (a): barter, since goods are swapped directly without money
Part (b): no, because money has to be accepted by everybody for payments, which one deal does not show

questions.q: Priya says, 'Only everyday things like salt and tea were ever used for exchange; the stone discs of Yap Island were never really accepted by anyone.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says Rai stones were used as money on Yap Island, the Tajadero in Central Mexico and the Tevau on the Solomon Islands, so unusual objects were accepted in their regions. Money is whatever people in a place commonly accept for payment, so 'only' is too strong.
s: Verdict: disagrees with the word 'only'
Names at least two unusual forms of money with their places
Links acceptance to the chapter's meaning of money as what everybody accepts

questions.q: Workers digging near an old market find a clay record of dealings: 'ten sacks of seed taken, six goats given; one cart-ride given, one bag of salt taken.' No coin is found with it. Which conclusion goes with the chapter?
questions.a: The record shows goods and services exchanged with no money, which is barter. The chapter says the barter system was the earliest form of exchange and that cattle, seeds and salt were among the commodities used. It does not say that money was unknown in the whole world.
o: The dealings are barter, the earliest form of exchange, using seeds, goats and salt
The people must have used the Rai stones for these dealings, since no coin was found with it
Money did not exist anywhere in the world at the time when this clay record was written
Goats and seeds were the money of every region of the world at that time in history

questions.q:
Class 7 held a Swap Day on the school lawn and the teacher noted five exchanges.
1. Rhea gave an old atlas and took a puzzle box.
2. Dev paid ₹35 at the stationery stall for a pencil box.
3. Zoya spent two hours helping a friend with homework and took a comic in return.
4. Ishaan gave a cricket glove and received ₹60 from Joy.
5. Neha gave a bag of toffees and took a bookmark.
(a) Which of the five exchanges are barter?
(b) Why is exchange 4 not barter, and what could Joy do to make it barter?
(c) Exchange 3 has no goods on Zoya's side. What does the chapter call what she gave, and is her deal still a transaction? Explain.
(d) Next year the committee must choose between 'goods and services only' and 'goods, services and rupee stalls'. Recommend one, giving a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 1, 3 and 5. (b) Joy paid ₹60, so money was the means of payment; she could give goods or a service that Ishaan wants. (c) Zoya gave a service. It is still a transaction, a piece of business between two people, done by barter without money. (d) Either choice is acceptable with a reason: goods and services only keeps the Swap Day purely barter, as in the book exchange club; adding rupee stalls lets people get things without finding someone who wants their goods.
s: Part (a): exchanges 1, 3 and 5 are barter
Part (b): exchange 4 uses money; Joy should give goods or a service instead
Part (c): Zoya gave a service, and it is a transaction done by barter
Part (d): a recommendation supported by a reason from the chapter

questions.q: Anil says, 'Barter means exchange of goods only.' Bela says, 'Barter means exchange without money.' Chitra says, 'Barter means exchange of goods and services without money.' Whose statement matches the chapter, and what is missing from the other two? Support your answer with one example of a service exchanged for goods.
questions.a: Chitra's statement matches the chapter. Anil leaves out services and also leaves out the condition that no money is used, so a swap paid in rupees would fit his words. Bela leaves out that goods and services are the things exchanged. Example: a tailor stitches a blouse for a neighbour and takes a basket of vegetables, which is a service swapped for goods.
s: Identifies Chitra's statement as the chapter's definition
Points out that Anil omits services and the no-money condition
Points out that Bela does not say what is exchanged
Gives a correct example of a service exchanged for goods

questions.q:
Arjun wrote three lines in his revision notes for the chapter 'From Barter to Money'.
Line 1: Barter is the exchange of goods and services without money.
Line 2: The Tevau, a coil of red feathers, was used as money in Central Mexico.
Line 3: Money is the common tool that everybody accepts.
His friend Sana says one line contradicts the chapter and another is incomplete.
(a) Which line contradicts the chapter, and what does the chapter say?
(b) Which line is incomplete, and what is missing from it?
(c) Arjun has room for only one list in his notes: the commodities used in barter, or the three unusual forms of money with their places. Which would help more in an exam answer on 'evidence of barter around the world'? Justify.
questions.a: (a) Line 2 contradicts the chapter: the Tevau was used as money on the Solomon Islands, while Central Mexico is where the copper Tajadero was used. (b) Line 3 is incomplete: it does not say what the common tool is used for, namely to make or receive payments in exchange for goods and services. (c) Either list is acceptable with a reason: the commodity list (cowrie shells, salt, tea, tobacco, cloth, cattle, seeds) shows how many everyday things were used for exchange, while the unusual forms with places show the evidence came from different parts of the world.
s: Part (a): Line 2, since the Tevau belongs to the Solomon Islands and Central Mexico had the Tajadero
Part (b): Line 3, which omits that money is used to make or receive payments for goods and services
Part (c): chooses one list and justifies with its use for the 'around the world' evidence

questions.q: Tara and a tailor agree that 12 kg of ripe mangoes is a fair price for a shirt, and the tailor wants mangoes. But the shirt will be ready only after ten days, and ripe mangoes will not last that long once kept. Which barter problem still stands in the way?
questions.a: Both sides want what the other has and they agree on the price, so the first two problems are settled, and mangoes can be weighed out in kilograms. What remains is that the fruit cannot be kept for long without spoiling, which is the problem of durability.
o: Durability, as the mangoes cannot be kept in good condition for ten days
Double coincidence of wants, as the tailor does not want mangoes
No common standard measure of value, as they cannot fix a price
Divisibility, as the mangoes cannot be split into smaller parts

questions.q: True or False: By exchanging his ox for several bags of wheat, the farmer was left with no barter problem, because wheat can be shared out in parts and kept in the shed until it is needed. Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. Wheat can be shared out in parts, so it eases the problem of divisibility, but the chapter says it cannot be stored for long because it rots or is eaten by rats, which is the problem of durability. The farmer must also carry the bags to the sellers.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: wheat can be divided but cannot be stored for long; it rots or is eaten by rats (durability)

questions.q:
Read the statements about the farmer's difficulties under barter.
1. In the farmer's story, the bags of wheat he received for his ox could be stored safely for a long time.
2. A person who owns an ox can pay for a sweater by handing over just a part of the ox.
3. Taking the ox from place to place is a problem that the chapter calls portability.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Only statement 3 is from the chapter. Statement 1 is false because the wheat rots or is eaten by rats, and statement 2 is false because the chapter says an ox cannot be exchanged in part for a sweater, which is the problem of divisibility.
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only

questions.q: In the farmer's story he exchanges his ox for several bags of wheat. (a) Which problem of the ox does this ease, and why? (b) Which problem does the wheat bring in?
questions.a: (a) Divisibility: an ox cannot be exchanged in part for a sweater, but bags of wheat can be shared out among the shoe-seller, the weaver and the chemist. (b) Durability: the wheat cannot be stored for long, as it would rot or be eaten by rats.
s: Part (a): divisibility, since wheat can be given in parts while an ox cannot
Part (b): durability, since wheat rots or is eaten by rats

questions.q: Four stalls at a haat each sell one thing and want another: Asha sells rice and wants salt; Bilal sells salt and wants cloth; Chitra sells cloth and wants salt; Dev sells shoes and wants rice. How many pairs of stalls can complete a direct swap with each other?
questions.a: Checking the six pairs, only Bilal and Chitra want what the other sells: Bilal wants cloth and Chitra sells it, Chitra wants salt and Bilal sells it. Every other pair fails the double coincidence of wants, for example Asha wants salt but Bilal wants cloth, not rice.
o: Exactly one pair
No pair at all
Exactly two pairs
Three pairs

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Fixing a common standard measure of value would not by itself make sure that a farmer finds someone who wants his ox.
Reason (R): A common standard measure of value tells how much one good is worth in terms of another, but it does not make another person want what one has.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true. A common measure of value (the chapter's agreed-upon worth) only settles the proportion of an exchange, while the double coincidence of wants is about whether the other person wants your goods; R states exactly why A holds.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Rohit says, 'If two people want each other's goods, the double coincidence of wants is solved, but barter can still fail because they may not agree on how much of one equals the other.' Do you agree? Use the chapter's example of shoes and wheat in your answer.
questions.a: Yes. Wanting each other's goods settles the double coincidence of wants, but the chapter says the proportion is then hard to settle because there is no common standard measure of value. In the farmer's story a discussion is needed to arrive at the fair amount of wheat for the shoes or for the sweater, and a person who feels the exchange is disadvantageous loses interest.
s: Verdict: agrees with Rohit
Reason: the proportion is hard to settle because there is no common standard measure of value
Example: the discussion about the fair amount of wheat for shoes or a sweater

questions.q: Sarla's family is paid 50 kg of ripe tomatoes for stitching work, but the next market is a week away and the tomatoes turn soft. A neighbour says, 'If they had paid you in money, you would have lost nothing.' Which function of money does the neighbour have in mind?
questions.a: The loss came from tomatoes not lasting, which is the problem of durability. The chapter says that money kept for a longer time can be used for purchases later, so the function is store of value. The other functions solve different problems.
o: Store of value, since money can be kept and used for purchases later
Medium of exchange, since every seller in the village accepts money
Common denomination, since money measures the value of all the goods
Standard of deferred payment, since money can be paid at a later date

questions.q: (a) In the farmer's story, the ox is first exchanged for wheat and then the wheat is exchanged for shoes, a sweater and medicines. Name one place where a double coincidence of wants must occur before the first step can happen. (b) Even when it does occur, the chapter says another problem can arise. Name it and say what it makes people do.
questions.a: (a) The farmer must find a person who wants an ox and is able to give bags of wheat, someone who both wants what he has and has what he wants. (b) There is no common standard measure of value, so it is hard to settle the proportion of the exchange, and a person who feels it is disadvantageous is not interested.
s: Part (a): finding someone who wants the ox and can give wheat
Part (b): no common standard measure of value, so the proportion is hard to settle and a person may lose interest

questions.q:
Match each problem of barter in Column A with the situation in Column B.
Column A: 1. Double coincidence of wants  2. No common standard measure of value  3. Divisibility  4. Durability
Column B: a. A weaver would give a shawl for wheat, but the wheat-owner wants only shoes.  b. A man who owns a single cow wants only a pair of slippers and cannot hand over a small part of it.  c. A farmer's wheat, taken in a swap for a goat, is half eaten by rats before the next market.  d. A weaver and a potter want each other's goods, but one thinks a shawl equals 4 pots and the other 9.
questions.a: The weaver and the wheat-owner who wants only shoes show a missing double coincidence of wants. The 4 pots against 9 pots show no common standard measure of value. A cow that cannot be handed over in part shows divisibility, and wheat eaten by rats shows durability.

questions.q: A farmer's ox is worth ₹24,000. The shoes he needs cost ₹1,500, the sweater ₹800 and the medicines ₹700. Wheat sells at ₹20 per kg. He weighs three plans. Plan 1: swap the ox for wheat worth ₹24,000 and pay the three sellers in wheat. Plan 2: find one person who wants the ox and will give just the three things for it. Plan 3: sell the ox for ₹24,000 in money and buy the three things. For each plan, work out what he is left with or loses, name the barter problem or the function of money that matters, and recommend one plan.
questions.a: Plan 1: the ox fetches 24,000 / 20 = 1,200 kg of wheat and the three things cost 3,000 / 20 = 150 kg, so 1,050 kg is left over, which he must carry (portability) and which rots or is eaten by rats (durability). Plan 2: he receives goods worth ₹3,000 for an ox worth ₹24,000, so he loses ₹21,000 because the ox cannot be handed over in part (divisibility). Plan 3: he keeps ₹21,000, which money lets him store and use later. Plan 3 is best because it avoids both losses.
s: Plan 1: 1,050 kg of wheat left over
Plan 1: portability and durability of the leftover wheat
Plan 2: loses ₹21,000, since the ox cannot be divided
Plan 3: keeps ₹21,000 as a store of value to use later
Recommends Plan 3 with a reason from the two comparisons

questions.q: Four students comment on the farmer's exchange of his ox for several bags of wheat. Which comment agrees with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the wheat solved part of the problem, since it can be shared out among the sellers, but it cannot be stored for long as it rots or is eaten by rats. The other comments claim the opposite or claim too much.
o: Wheat can be shared out in parts for the three sellers, but cannot be stored for long
Wheat can be kept in the shed for years, so the farmer need not worry about storing it
Wheat is worse than the ox because bags of wheat cannot be exchanged in parts
Wheat ends the farmer's difficulties because the shoe-seller, weaver and chemist will accept it

questions.q: In the farmer's story he exchanges the ox for wheat, and then gives wheat to the shoe-seller, the sweater-seller and the person selling medicines separately. (a) How many exchanges must he complete in all? (b) Why does the chapter say a discussion must take place in the wheat exchanges, and which barter problem causes it?
questions.a: (a) 1 + 3 = 4 exchanges. (b) In each wheat exchange the two sides must arrive at the fair amount of wheat for the item, which is hard because there is no common standard measure of value.
s: Part (a): 4 exchanges (one for wheat and three for the items)
Part (b): a fair amount must be agreed each time, because there is no common standard measure of value

questions.q: Mohan owns one buffalo, worth about 8 sacks of rice. He needs only 1 sack of rice today. Show why he cannot complete this exchange by giving part of his buffalo, name the problem, and say what he would be left with if he gives the whole buffalo.
questions.a: He would have to give one-eighth of the buffalo, which cannot be cut off without destroying its value. This is the problem of divisibility. If he gives the whole buffalo he gets 8 sacks and must carry and store 7 sacks he does not need today, which brings the problems of portability and durability.
s: Shows that only one-eighth of a buffalo would be needed and cannot be separated
Names the problem as divisibility
States that giving the whole buffalo leaves him with 7 extra sacks to carry and store

questions.q:
At the Dindori weekly market, Bhima has one goat and wants shoes, a sweater and medicines. In barter, the traders' rates are 15 kg of wheat for the shoes, 20 kg for the sweater and 5 kg for the medicines. A grain trader offers 70 kg of wheat for the goat, while a cattle dealer offers ₹2,400 in cash. Wheat sells at ₹30 per kg in the market.
(a) Which barter problem stops Bhima from giving just part of his goat, and after buying all three things with wheat how many kilograms of wheat will he still have?
(b) Name the two barter problems that this leftover wheat will give him.
(c) If he takes the ₹2,400 and pays the traders the rupee value of the same wheat rates, how much money is left, and which function of money lets him keep it for later?
(d) Compare the leftover wheat with the leftover cash and recommend which offer Bhima should accept, with a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Divisibility, as a goat cannot be handed over in part; 70 - (15 + 20 + 5) = 30 kg of wheat is left. (b) Portability, since he has to carry it, and durability, since it can rot or be eaten by rats. (c) The three items cost 40 kg x ₹30 = ₹1,200, so ₹1,200 is left from the ₹2,400; money acts as a store of value, so he can keep it and use it later. (d) The leftover wheat is worth 30 x ₹30 = ₹900, which is ₹300 less than the ₹1,200 cash; cash is also easy to carry and does not rot, so he should accept the cash offer.
s: Part (a): divisibility, and 30 kg of wheat left
Part (b): portability and durability
Part (c): ₹1,200 left, kept as a store of value
Part (d): cash chosen, with ₹1,200 against wheat worth ₹900 and the lack of carrying or rotting trouble

questions.q: At a haat, three families each swap one goat of the same age and health for wheat. Family A gets 20 kg, family B gets 14 kg and family C gets 26 kg. Which barter problem does this 12 kg spread between the lowest and highest deal best show?
questions.a: Equal goats fetched very different amounts of wheat, so nothing agreed fixes how much wheat a goat is worth; this is the lack of a common standard measure of value. The goats could all be swapped and wheat is divisible, so the other problems do not explain the spread.
o: No common standard measure of value
Lack of double coincidence of wants
Lack of divisibility of the goat
Lack of durability of the wheat

questions.q: (a) At a weekly haat, a basket-maker wants a cooking pot and the potter wants a basket. The basket is worth far more than one pot, and the two cannot agree on how many pots equal one basket. Which two barter problems appear? (b) Which of them does the chapter say could be removed by pricing both goods in money?
questions.a: (a) Divisibility, since the potter cannot hand over a part of the basket to make up the difference, and the lack of a common standard measure of value, since they cannot agree how many pots equal one basket. (b) Pricing both in money gives a common standard measure of value, so the worth of a basket and a pot can be compared.
s: Part (a): divisibility and no common standard measure of value
Part (b): money prices act as a common measure so worth can be compared

questions.q: 'Money makes the farmer's situation easier.' Justify this statement by choosing any three problems of barter and explaining how money removes each one. Then show how the farmer would complete his shopping for shoes, a sweater and medicines using money.
questions.a: Double coincidence of wants: money is accepted by everybody, so he need not find someone who wants an ox. Common standard measure of value: prices in money let the ox, shoes and sweater be compared. Portability and durability: money is easy to carry and can be kept for a long time instead of rotting wheat. Shopping: he sells the ox for money, then pays the cobbler, the weaver and the chemist separately and keeps what remains for later.
s: First problem with how money removes it
Second problem with how money removes it
Third problem with how money removes it
Describes selling the ox for money
Describes paying the three sellers one by one and keeping the rest

questions.q: Write a short story of four or five lines about a milk seller in a village where only barter is used, which shows the problem of durability. End with one line on how money would help.
questions.a: Example: Kamla gets a sack of grain from the weaver for her milk, but the next day the milk she was keeping for another trader has gone sour, and she cannot keep the grain safe from rats. With money she could sell the milk at once and keep the rupees to spend later.
s: A story where a good is spoilt or damaged while being kept
The spoilage is clearly the problem of durability
One line saying money can be kept and used later

questions.q:
At a village haat, Lata has one sealed sack of rice worth ₹800 and no other goods. Gopal has an oil lamp worth ₹500 and wants cloth. Farida has one stitched shawl worth ₹800 and wants rice. The sack must be taken whole, the shawl cannot be cut and the lamp cannot be split. A trader at the haat is ready to buy the sack for ₹800 in cash.
(a) Can Lata and Gopal complete a direct swap? Give the reason.
(b) Describe a chain of two exchanges after which Lata has the lamp.
(c) In that chain Lata hands over the shawl worth ₹800 for a lamp worth ₹500. Which barter problem stops Gopal from giving back the extra value, and how much does Lata lose?
(d) Lata could instead sell the sack to the trader for ₹800 and pay Gopal ₹500 for the lamp. Compare the two routes and recommend one.
questions.a: (a) No, Gopal wants cloth, not rice. (b) Lata gives her sack to Farida and takes the shawl, then gives the shawl to Gopal and takes the lamp. (c) Divisibility: the lamp (and the shawl) cannot be split to return the difference, and Gopal has nothing else to give; she loses ₹800 - ₹500 = ₹300 of value. (d) With rupees she pays ₹500 for the lamp and keeps ₹300, while the chain loses ₹300 of value, so the money route is better.
s: Part (a): no, since Gopal wants cloth and not rice
Part (b): sack to Farida for the shawl, then shawl to Gopal for the lamp
Part (c): divisibility and a loss of ₹300
Part (d): money route keeps ₹300 against a loss of ₹300 in the chain

questions.q: A reporter's note says: 'The Junbeel Mela is a one-day fair at Junbeel in Morigaon district of Assam. It begins with a feast, and it started in the 15th century as a gathering of the chiefs of the Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia communities.' How many details in the note disagree with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says the mela lasts three days, and that it begins with the Agni Puja, the worship of fire, not a feast. The place and the 15th-century gathering of the four communities' chiefs are as the chapter gives them, so two details are wrong.
o: Two: how long the fair lasts and how it begins
One: only how long the fair lasts
Three: its length, its opening and when it started
None: every detail in the note agrees

questions.q: Suppose no family from the hills comes to the Junbeel Mela one year, though the plains families arrive as usual. (a) Which exchange described in the chapter cannot take place? (b) Name one thing the plains families go without and one thing the absent hill families go without.
questions.a: (a) The exchange of handmade goods and artifacts made from the forests of the hills for rice cakes and other food. (b) The plains families go without those handmade goods; the hill families go without rice cakes and other foods that cannot be grown in the hills.
s: Part (a): hill handmade goods for rice cakes and other foods of the plains
Part (b): plains lose the handmade goods and hill families lose the foods they cannot grow

questions.q: A hill family takes 7 handmade mats to the Junbeel Mela on every day that the fair runs and swaps all of them for rice cakes. Over one whole mela it swaps ___ mats.
A newspaper report calls the Junbeel Mela 'only a commercial market that lasts three days'. Which detail from the chapter shows the report leaves out something important about the fair?
questions.a: The chapter calls the mela a socio-cultural fair. It grew out of yearly gatherings of the chiefs of the Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia communities, who met from the 15th century to discuss political issues and keep friendly relations. The other details describe the fair's name, place and morning barter, which do not show anything beyond trade.
o: It began with yearly gatherings of chiefs of four tribal communities
Its name joins the Assamese words for the moon and for a wetland
It is held every year at Junbeel in the Morigaon district of Assam
Bartering of roots, fruit and herbs begins early every morning there

questions.q: Sumit says, 'Because the Junbeel Mela begins with the Agni Puja, it is a religious ceremony and not a place of trade.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter calls the mela a socio-cultural fair, so the Agni Puja, a prayer for universal wellbeing, is only one part of it. It also grew from the yearly gathering of the chiefs, and bartering of roots, vegetables, fruit, herbs and spices begins early in the morning, with hill goods exchanged for rice cakes. So it is both a cultural event and a place of trade.
s: Verdict: disagrees, since the puja is only the opening of a socio-cultural fair
Evidence of trade: early-morning barter of local produce or hill goods for rice cakes
Evidence of the wider fair: the chiefs' gathering or the combination of culture and trade

questions.q: Suppose the chiefs of the Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia communities had never begun their yearly meetings in the 15th century. Which part of the chapter's account would then have had no starting point?
questions.a: The chapter says people began to gather around the chiefs' meeting and brought their produce, and it soon turned into a fair. So the Junbeel Mela depends on the meeting. The vendor's practice, the Rai stones and the book exchange are described without any link to it.
o: The Junbeel Mela, which grew out of the chiefs' meeting
The vendor's practice of swapping new utensils for old clothes at people's homes
The use of the Rai stones as money in the Pacific country of Micronesia
The book exchange club, in which friends trade the books they have finished

questions.q: In the vendor's practice, the households gain by getting rid of items they no longer need. (a) What does the vendor gain? (b) At the Junbeel Mela the hill families gain foods that cannot be grown in the hills. What do the plains families gain from the same exchange?
questions.a: (a) The vendor collects used clothes and fabrics that can be resold, repurposed or recycled. (b) The plains families gain the handmade goods and artifacts made from natural materials taken from the forests of the hills.
s: Part (a): cloth that can be resold, repurposed or recycled
Part (b): handmade goods and artifacts made from forest materials

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Exchanging old clothes for new utensils benefits both the household and the vendor.
Reason (R): The household collects cloth that can be resold, repurposed or recycled, while the vendor gets rid of items he no longer needs.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true: the household clears things it no longer needs and the vendor collects materials. R is false because it swaps the two sides: it is the vendor who collects the cloth and the household that gets rid of unneeded items.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A vendor visits a Hyderabad apartment block offering steel utensils for old clothes, with no cash paid: 1 mug for every 1 kg of clothes, 1 plate for every 2 kg and 1 bucket for every 5 kg. Mrs Iyer has 6 kg of old clothes.
(a) Why is this exchange barter, and what does the vendor gain?
(b) What weight of clothes is needed for one bucket and one plate, and by how much is Mrs Iyer short?
(c) Which bucket-and-small-utensil combination uses her 6 kg exactly?
(d) Her daughter wants to keep 2 kg of the clothes for a school project. Can Mrs Iyer still take the bucket? Decide whether she should give all 6 kg or only 4 kg, and say what she can take if she gives 4 kg.
questions.a: (a) Goods are exchanged for goods without money; the vendor collects cloth that can be resold, repurposed or recycled. (b) 5 + 2 = 7 kg, so she is 1 kg short. (c) One bucket and one mug: 5 + 1 = 6 kg. (d) With 4 kg she cannot take the bucket (5 kg), but can take 2 plates, or 1 plate and 2 mugs, or 4 mugs. Either decision is acceptable with a reason: giving all 6 kg clears more unwanted clothes and gets a bucket, while keeping 2 kg meets her daughter's need but loses the bucket.
s: Part (a): barter because no money is used; the vendor gains reusable cloth
Part (b): 7 kg needed and 1 kg short
Part (c): one bucket and one mug
Part (d): 4 kg cannot buy the bucket, with a reasoned decision and an option she can take

questions.q: Which of these is closest in idea to the chapter's practice of exchanging old clothes for new utensils?
questions.a: In the practice, a visiting seller gives something useful in return for used things that he can resell or recycle, with no money. A scrap dealer giving a bowl for old newspapers does the same. A cash sale uses money, a bank pays interest in money, and a free gift is not an exchange.
o: A scrap dealer gives a steel bowl in return for a household's old newspapers, which he sells on
A shopkeeper sells a steel bowl to a household for ₹150 in cash at his shop counter
A bank adds interest to a household's savings account at the end of each year
A household gives its old clothes to a relative and asks for nothing in return

questions.q:
Read the statements about the Junbeel Mela and barter today.
1. The chiefs of the Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia communities began to gather in the 15th century at Junbeel to organise trade fairs.
2. The Junbeel Mela begins with the Agni Puja, the worship of fire, as a prayer for universal wellbeing.
3. In the old-clothes-for-utensils practice, households get rid of items they no longer need while vendors collect materials that can be resold, repurposed or recycled.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 1 is false: the chiefs gathered to discuss political issues and to maintain friendly relationships, and the fair grew later as people brought their produce.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q: A student writes: 'The Junbeel Mela began as a fair; later, the chiefs of the Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia communities started gathering there each year.' (a) Correct the order of events using the chapter. (b) State the purpose of the chiefs' yearly gathering.
questions.a: (a) The chiefs began to gather first, from the 15th century; people then gathered around the event and brought their produce, and it turned into a fair. (b) To discuss political issues and to maintain friendly relationships.
s: Part (a): the chiefs' gathering came first and the fair grew out of it
Part (b): to discuss political issues and keep friendly relationships

questions.q: Write a four-line notice for a 'Toy Exchange Club' in your colony that follows the idea of the book exchange club in the chapter. Say what members bring, what they take away and why nobody needs to spend any money.
questions.a: Example: Bring toys your child has outgrown to the community hall on Sunday at 10 a.m. and choose another toy from the collection. Swap, do not buy: each toy goes to a new child, so no rupee is needed.
s: Members bring something they no longer need
Members take something else away
States that the exchange needs no money

questions.q: Aman says, 'The Junbeel Mela proves that money has not replaced barter anywhere; barter is still the main way of exchange across the whole country.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says money has replaced traditional barter systems all around the world, although some barter systems still exist, and the Junbeel Mela is one of them. It does not call barter the main method today.
o: Money has replaced barter around the world, but a few systems like the mela remain
He is right, since the chapter calls barter the main method of exchange across the country
He is wrong, since the chapter says the mela uses rupees for every trade made there
He is wrong, since the chapter says the mela's barter ended in the 15th century

questions.q: A visitor says, 'The Junbeel Mela is mainly a market; the Agni Puja and the chiefs' gathering are only decoration.' Write a reply that argues against this, using at least four points from the chapter.
questions.a: The chapter calls the mela a socio-cultural fair, so it is more than a market. It grew out of the yearly gathering of the chiefs of the Tiwa, Karbi, Khasi and Jaintia communities, which began in the 15th century to discuss political issues and keep friendly relationships. It begins with the Agni Puja, the worship of fire, a prayer for universal wellbeing. Trade came as people gathered and brought their produce, and bartering of roots, vegetables, fruit, herbs and spices begins early in the morning, with hill goods exchanged for rice cakes. So the culture and the gathering are part of what the mela is, and the trade grew from them.
s: Calls the mela socio-cultural and takes a position against the visitor
Chiefs' gathering from the 15th century for political issues and friendly relationships
Agni Puja as a prayer for universal wellbeing at the beginning
Trade grew after people gathered and brought produce, with early-morning barter of local products
Hill handmade goods exchanged for rice cakes, and a conclusion that culture and trade belong together

questions.q: Radha says, 'A book exchange club cannot be called barter, because nobody there sells anything.' Reply using the chapter.
questions.a: Barter is the exchange of goods without money, and in the club friends swap one book for another without spending money, so it is barter. Nobody needs to sell for it to be barter.
s: Barter means exchange without money, not selling
Applies it to books swapped for books without spending money

questions.q:
At the Junbeel Mela, Pranab's hill family gave 8 baskets, handmade from forest materials, to a plains family and took 48 rice cakes. Later he has 9 more baskets. Stall A offers 6 rice cakes for each basket. Stall B offers 5 rice cakes and one bundle of dried herbs for each basket.
(a) Was the first exchange barter, and at what rate, in rice cakes per basket, was it done?
(b) How many rice cakes will Stall A give for the 9 baskets?
(c) Compare what the two stalls offer for 9 baskets, and name the barter problem that makes it hard to say which is worth more.
(d) The family needs food for the next three days and also wants herbs for pickle. Recommend a stall and justify it.
questions.a: (a) Yes, baskets for rice cakes with no money; 48 / 8 = 6 rice cakes per basket. (b) 9 x 6 = 54 rice cakes. (c) Stall A gives 54 rice cakes; Stall B gives 45 rice cakes and 9 bundles of herbs. The family gets 9 fewer rice cakes at B for 9 bundles; with no common standard measure of value one cannot say whether a bundle is worth more than a rice cake. (d) Either stall is acceptable with a reason: A for the most food, B if the herbs are valued at more than the 9 cakes given up.
s: Part (a): barter, at 6 rice cakes per basket
Part (b): 54 rice cakes
Part (c): 54 against 45 plus 9 bundles, with the missing common standard measure of value
Part (d): a stall recommended with a reason tied to the family's needs

questions.q: A vendor gives 1 bucket for every 6 kg of old clothes, 1 plate for every 3 kg and 1 spoon set for every 1 kg. Show that a household with 14 kg of clothes cannot take 2 buckets and 2 plates. Then give one combination that uses exactly 14 kg and includes a bucket, and say why the vendor wants the clothes.
questions.a: 2 buckets need 12 kg and 2 plates need 6 kg, which is 18 kg, and 18 is more than 14, so it is impossible. One combination is 2 buckets and 2 spoon sets (12 + 2 = 14 kg), or 1 bucket, 2 plates and 2 spoon sets (6 + 6 + 2 = 14 kg). The vendor collects cloth that can be resold, repurposed or recycled.
s: Shows 12 + 6 = 18 kg, which is more than 14 kg
Gives a correct combination using exactly 14 kg with at least one bucket
States that the vendor gains cloth to resell, repurpose or recycle

questions.q: A colony's book exchange club has 24 members. Each member brings 3 books and takes home 3 different books. (a) How many books are on the shelf when the exchange begins, and how many can a member choose from if she may not take her own 3? (b) Which word of the chapter describes what the members do, and what does each gain?
questions.a: (a) 24 x 3 = 72 books on the shelf, and 72 - 3 = 69 to choose from. (b) It is barter: books are swapped for books without money, and each member gets new stories without spending any money.
s: Part (a): 72 books and 69 to choose from
Part (b): barter, with new stories gained without spending money

questions.q: 'Barter has not vanished; it survives where it suits the people involved.' Justify this statement using the three examples of barter today given in the chapter.
questions.a: At the Junbeel Mela, hill people get food they cannot grow, such as rice cakes, by exchanging their own produce and handmade goods. In the book exchange club, friends get new stories without spending any money. In the old-clothes-for-utensils practice, households get rid of things they no longer need and the vendor gets material to reuse. In each case both sides get what they want without money, so barter continues where it works for them.
s: Junbeel Mela example linked to a need the hills cannot meet
Book exchange club example
Old clothes for utensils example
Explains that both sides gain without money in these cases

questions.q:
Read the statements about the functions of money.
1. Money is accepted as a way of making deferred payments, which makes it a standard of deferred payment.
2. The money that parents pay a shopkeeper is used by him to pay his workers, who spend the same money on everyday essentials.
3. Money acts as a store of value because it is accepted for payments that are made at a later date.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 are from the chapter. Statement 3 mixes up two functions: a payment made at a later date is the standard of deferred payment, while a store of value means money can be kept and used for purchases later.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Rhea saves ₹100 a month for five months and then buys headphones for ₹500. Sam takes the same headphones today and agrees to pay ₹500 after five months. Which statement matches the chapter?
questions.a: Rhea keeps her money and spends it later, which is money as a store of value. Sam gets the goods first and pays later, which is money as a standard of deferred payment. The other statements swap or merge the two.
o: Rhea relies on money as a store of value, and Sam on money as a standard of deferred payment
Rhea relies on money as a standard of deferred payment, and Sam on money as a store of value
Both rely on money only as a medium of exchange, because both buy the same headphones
Both rely on money as a store of value, because both wait five months for the purchase

questions.q: A geometry set costs ₹240. Neha pays ₹90 on the day and promises the balance on Monday. Rani takes a set and pays the whole ₹240 on Monday. (a) Which function of money lets both girls take the set today? (b) What fraction of the price is still unpaid on the day for each girl?
questions.a: (a) The standard of deferred payment, since money is accepted as a way of making payments later. (b) Neha owes ₹240 - ₹90 = ₹150, which is 150/240 = 5/8 of the price; Rani owes the whole price, 240/240 = 1.
s: Part (a): standard of deferred payment
Part (b): 5/8 for Neha and the whole price for Rani

questions.q: Maya puts ₹50 a week in a tin for six weeks and then buys a ₹300 school bag with it. The tin works because money acts as a ___.
questions.a: store of value

questions.q: Leela says, 'Money's work as a medium of exchange is only for buying things in shops; it plays no part in paying wages.' Do you agree? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says the money parents pay to shopkeepers is used by the shopkeepers to pay salaries to their workers, so the accepted method of payment also carries wages. The workers then use the same medium to buy everyday essentials and pay their children's school fees.
s: Verdict: disagrees with Leela
Wages: shopkeepers use the money they receive to pay salaries to workers
Workers spend the same medium on essentials or school fees

questions.q: Mr Shah, a tailor, gets ₹1,200 from a customer for a suit and puts ₹1,000 of it in a cupboard to buy cloth next season. Which two functions of money has he used, in that order?
questions.a: The customer's payment for the suit shows money as a medium of exchange, and keeping ₹1,000 aside to buy cloth later shows money as a store of value. The other orders reverse them or bring in functions that do not match.
o: Medium of exchange, then store of value
Store of value, then medium of exchange
Common denomination, then standard of deferred payment
Standard of deferred payment, then common denomination

questions.q: True or False: In the chapter's example, the money that parents pay to shopkeepers stays with the shopkeepers, because shopkeepers are the last people to receive it. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the shopkeepers use that money to pay salaries to their workers, and the workers use the same medium to buy everyday essentials and pay school fees, so the money keeps moving from person to person.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: shopkeepers pay salaries and the workers spend the same money on essentials and fees

questions.q:
Match each function of money in Column A with the situation in Column B.
Column A: 1. Medium of exchange  2. Standard of deferred payment  3. Store of value  4. Common denomination
Column B: a. Zara's uncle gives her ₹2,000 in January and she leaves it untouched to buy a bicycle in June.  b. A shopkeeper lets Mohan take school shoes costing ₹900 now if he pays the full amount at the end of the month.  c. A customer works out which is dearer per kilogram, 2 kg of apples at ₹260 or 3 kg of grapes at ₹240.  d. A tailor accepts ₹700 for a suit because the grocer, the landlord and the school will all accept it from him.
questions.a: The tailor's ₹700 accepted by everyone is the medium of exchange. Taking shoes now and paying at the month-end is deferred payment. Leaving the ₹2,000 untouched until June is the store of value. Comparing apples and grapes in rupees per kilogram uses money as a common denomination.

questions.q: A buyer takes a bicycle priced ₹2,000, pays ₹800 today and agrees to clear the balance in 3 equal monthly parts. How much is each monthly part, and which function of money does the arrangement rely on?
questions.a: The balance is 2,000 - 800 = 1,200, and 1,200 / 3 = 400 a month. Paying part of the price later for goods already taken is the standard of deferred payment.
o: ₹400 a month, with money as a standard of deferred payment
₹400 a month, with money as a store of value
₹600 a month, with money as a standard of deferred payment
₹667 a month, with money as a common denomination

questions.q: (a) In the chapter's chain, parents pay shopkeepers and shopkeepers pay their workers. Name two things the workers do with the same money. (b) Suppose each shopkeeper would take only one kind of goods as payment. Which function of money would then be missing, and what would the workers have to do?
questions.a: (a) They buy everyday essentials and other goods, and pay their children's school fees. (b) The medium of exchange, an accepted method of payment, would be missing, so each worker would have to find sellers who want the particular goods he can offer, as in barter.
s: Part (a): two uses such as essentials and school fees
Part (b): the medium of exchange is missing, so workers must find sellers who want the goods they offer

questions.q:
Mr Joseph's stationery shop sells a geometry box for ₹95, an atlas for ₹180 and an art kit for ₹220. Rohit has ₹200 and needs the atlas and the geometry box. Mr Joseph tells him he may take both today, pay ₹200 now and pay the balance on Monday. Another shop nearby sells the atlas for ₹170 and the box for ₹90 but accepts only cash.
(a) Which function of money lets Rohit add two different goods into one total, and what is the total price of the atlas and the box at Mr Joseph's shop?
(b) Name the function of money that lets Rohit take both today, and state the balance due on Monday.
(c) What is the total at the other shop, and by how much is it lower than Mr Joseph's? By how much is Rohit's ₹200 short of it?
(d) Which shop should Rohit choose? Give a decision using your figures and the function of money named in (b).
questions.a: (a) Common denomination; ₹95 + ₹180 = ₹275. (b) Standard of deferred payment; the balance is ₹275 - ₹200 = ₹75. (c) ₹170 + ₹90 = ₹260, which is ₹15 lower, but ₹260 - ₹200 = ₹60 more than he has, and the shop takes only cash. (d) Either shop is acceptable with a reason: Mr Joseph's lets him take both today with ₹75 deferred to Monday for ₹15 more; the cheaper shop saves ₹15 but he can pay only ₹200 there, so he would have to leave one item or come back with ₹60 more.
s: Part (a): common denomination and ₹275
Part (b): deferred payment and a balance of ₹75
Part (c): ₹260, ₹15 lower, and ₹60 beyond Rohit's ₹200
Part (d): a choice justified with the ₹15 saving, the ₹60 shortfall and deferred payment

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Wheat is as good a store of value for a farmer as money is, since it can be kept and used for purchases later.
Reason (R): Wheat rots or is eaten by rats if it is stored for long.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is false: money can be kept for a longer time and used later, but wheat cannot be stored for long. R is true, and it is the very reason A fails.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.q: A trader's father swapped three kinds of goods within his own village. The trader now deals in many kinds of goods and travels to far-off villages. (a) Using the chapter, give two reasons why barter became harder for the trader than for his father. (b) Which function of money lets a seller in a far village accept the trader's payment?
questions.a: (a) The types and numbers of things being exchanged grew, and the distances across which exchange took place became longer. (b) The medium of exchange: money is the accepted method of payment.
s: Part (a): more kinds and numbers of goods, and longer distances
Part (b): medium of exchange

questions.q: Write a short situation at a school fair stall in which money acts (i) as a medium of exchange and (ii) as a common denomination. Mention a price in rupees for each.
questions.a: Example: Meena pays ₹30 for a plate of pakoras at the stall (medium of exchange). She compares the pakoras at ₹30 with a cup of lemonade at ₹15 and finds that the pakoras cost twice as much (common denomination).
s: Situation with a payment in rupees as medium of exchange
Situation comparing two prices as common denomination
Rupee amounts that are consistent in the comparison

questions.q:
In one week: on Monday, Mrs Pillai pays the grocer ₹850 for vegetables. On Tuesday the grocer pays his helper Ravi ₹1,200 as wages. On Wednesday Ravi buys shoes priced ₹900, pays ₹700 and promises the balance on Saturday. After paying that balance on Saturday, he puts the rest of his wages in a tin for next month's school fees. The grocer's board shows tomatoes at ₹40 per kg and onions at ₹30 per kg.
(a) Name the function of money in the Monday and Tuesday payments and say why the same money keeps moving.
(b) Name the function on Wednesday and the balance due on Saturday.
(c) Name the function shown by the tin and the amount in it.
(d) Name the function shown by the board and how much dearer a kilogram of tomatoes is than a kilogram of onions.
questions.a: (a) Medium of exchange: the customer's payment reaches the grocer and the grocer uses it to pay Ravi, because everyone accepts it as payment. (b) Standard of deferred payment; the balance is ₹900 - ₹700 = ₹200. (c) Store of value; ₹1,200 - ₹700 - ₹200 = ₹300 is in the tin. (d) Common denomination; ₹40 - ₹30 = ₹10 dearer.
s: Part (a): medium of exchange
Part (a): the same money passes from customer to grocer to helper because everyone accepts it
Part (b): standard of deferred payment and a balance of ₹200
Part (c): store of value and ₹300
Part (d): common denomination and ₹10 dearer

questions.q: A student writes in her notes, 'The board at the vegetable stall says tomatoes ₹40 per kg, so money is working as a medium of exchange here.' Which correction is best?
questions.a: The board only states the value of tomatoes in rupees, so goods can be compared in one unit, which is the common denomination. Money works as a medium of exchange only when it is actually handed over as payment.
o: The board shows money as a common denomination; the medium of exchange comes when payment is made
The board shows money as a store of value, because the price is fixed until the stall closes
The board shows money as a standard of deferred payment, because customers can pay later
No correction is needed, because every use of money is a medium of exchange

questions.q: Differentiate money as a store of value from money as a standard of deferred payment by giving one example of each, and say in each example whether the money or the goods come first.
questions.a: Store of value: a farmer keeps money from his crop and buys things next month, so the money comes first and the goods are bought later. Standard of deferred payment: a shopper takes a book today and pays the rest next week, so the goods come first and the payment later.
s: Store of value: an example in which money is kept first and goods are bought later
Standard of deferred payment: an example in which goods are taken first and money paid later

questions.q: In barter, a cobbler and a rice seller cannot say how many bags of rice a pair of shoes is worth. Show how prices in money settle this if a pair of shoes costs ₹600 and a 2 kg bag of rice costs ₹120, and name the function of money you used.
questions.a: 600 / 120 = 5, so the shoes are worth 5 bags of rice. Prices in one unit make the two goods comparable; the function is the common denomination.
s: Divides ₹600 by ₹120
States that the shoes equal 5 bags
Names the common denomination function

questions.q: Shruti sells her old bicycle to a neighbour for ₹3,000 and uses ₹800 of it to buy a school bag from a shop. Show how money acted as a medium of exchange in both steps, and say what the bag seller would have had to want under barter.
questions.a: The neighbour pays rupees that Shruti accepts for the bicycle, and the shop accepts the same rupees as payment for the bag. Under barter the bag seller would have had to want a bicycle (or something else Shruti owned).
s: Rupees accepted as payment for the bicycle, then for the bag
Under barter the bag seller would have had to want what Shruti owned

questions.q:
Mr Das's grocery shop received ₹48,000 last month from 20 families, each paying the same amount. He spent ₹27,000 on goods from the wholesaler, paid ₹7,500 to each of his two helpers and ₹4,000 as shop rent. His helpers use their pay for rent, groceries and school fees.
(a) Which function of money lets each shop accept the helpers' pay as payment, and how much did each family pay?
(b) How much money was left with Mr Das after all these payments?
(c) Name the function of money that lets Mr Das keep the remainder for later, and the barter problem he would face if he had saved it as sacks of grain.
(d) Mr Das can raise each helper's pay by ₹500 or keep the whole remainder as savings. Which should he choose? Justify using the functions of money.
questions.a: (a) Medium of exchange; ₹48,000 / 20 = ₹2,400. (b) ₹48,000 - ₹27,000 - ₹15,000 - ₹4,000 = ₹2,000. (c) Store of value; as sacks of grain it would rot or be eaten by rats, which is durability. (d) Either choice is acceptable with a reason: a raise costs 2 x ₹500 = ₹1,000 and leaves ₹1,000 saved, and the helpers' extra pay passes on through the shops; keeping all ₹2,000 as a store of value gives a bigger cushion for future costs.
s: Part (a): medium of exchange and ₹2,400
Part (b): ₹2,000 left
Part (c): store of value, and durability of stored grain
Part (d): a decision using the functions and the ₹1,000 cost of the raise

questions.q: A farmer must keep the value of his harvest until the next season. Compare wheat and money as ways of doing this, using the chapter's story. Which would you advise him to use, and why?
questions.a: Wheat cannot be stored for long: it rots or is eaten by rats, and it has to be carried each time he needs something. Money can be kept for a longer time and used for purchases later, so it acts as a store of value. It also works because everybody accepts it. I would advise money, though he should still keep enough wheat for his family's food.
s: States the limits of wheat: rotting, rats and carrying
States that money can be kept longer and used later
Adds that money works because everybody accepts it
Gives a clear recommendation
Supports it with a reason that fits the farmer's case

questions.q:
Read the statements about coins.
1. The minting and issue of ancient coins was controlled entirely by the rulers of the kingdoms.
2. Today's coins are alloys consisting largely of iron, with other materials such as chromium, silicon and carbon in precise proportions.
3. In ancient times the two sides of a coin, the head (obverse) and the tail (reverse), carried different kinds of symbols and motifs.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are given in the chapter: rulers controlled the minting entirely, today's coins are alloys largely of iron with chromium, silicon and carbon, and the two sides of ancient coins carried different symbols and motifs.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q: A student writes: 'Ancient Indian coins were all pure gold, and the coins we use today are all pure copper.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says ancient coins were made from precious metals like gold, silver and copper or their alloys, and that today's coins are also alloys, consisting largely of iron with chromium, silicon and carbon.
o: Ancient coins used gold, silver, copper or alloys; today's are alloys largely of iron
Both ancient and modern coins used pure metals, but the metals in them were different ones
Ancient coins were alloys of iron, and today's coins are made of gold and silver in alloy
Only the modern coins were made of metals, as ancient coins were made of baked clay

questions.q: A museum card lists four coins. Coin P: silver, a tiger emblem, dated 850 to 1279 CE. Coin Q: a Varaha image on one side and a decorated three-tiered parasol on the other. Coin R: Roman gold with a king's head, dug up at Pudukkottai. Coin S: a tree on one face and a hill on the other. (a) Which two coins carry nature motifs? (b) Which coin gives evidence of southern India's trade with other lands, and what do scholars conclude from it?
questions.a: (a) Coin P (an animal, the tiger) and Coin S (a tree and a hill). (b) Coin R, the Roman gold coin; scholars conclude that southern India traded with the rest of the world and that the trade was in favour of India.
s: Part (a): coins P and S, whose motifs are an animal, a tree and a hill
Part (b): coin R, showing trade with the world that was in favour of India

questions.q: A coin shows a king's portrait on one face and a tree on the other. Using the glossary's meaning of 'obverse' as the side that bears the head, the tree face is the coin's ___.
questions.a: reverse

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Scholars take the Roman gold coins found at Pudukkottai as a sign of southern India's trade with the rest of the world.
Reason (R): Coins issued by rulers of another land were found far from that land, in parts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, and R explains A: coins of Roman kings turning up in southern India is the finding from which scholars infer trade between the two regions.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Two students answer the question 'What do the Roman gold coins found at Pudukkottai show?' Ila says, 'Rome must have ruled southern India.' Manoj says, 'Southern India traded with distant lands, and the trade favoured India.' Whose answer matches the chapter? Say what is wrong with the other.
questions.a: Manoj's. The chapter uses these finds to show that southern India traded with the rest of the world, and scholars conclude the trade was in favour of India. Ila's conclusion is not supported: coins found in a place show contact and trade, not rule.
s: Identifies Manoj's answer
States the chapter's conclusion: trade with the rest of the world, in favour of India
Explains why Ila's claim fails: coins show trade, not rule

questions.q: In 1947 Seema has 6 half-anna coins and 2 quarter-anna coins. Using the chapter's price for bananas in 1947, how many bananas can she buy?
questions.a: A half-anna is half of an anna and a quarter-anna is a quarter of an anna, so she has 6 x 1/2 + 2 x 1/4 = 3.5 annas. One anna bought a dozen bananas, so 3.5 x 12 = 42 bananas. Ignoring the quarter-annas gives 36, treating each coin as an anna gives 96, and treating a quarter-anna as a half-anna gives 48.
o: 42 bananas
36 bananas
96 bananas
48 bananas

questions.q: (a) Why were alloys used to make coins, according to the chapter's glossary? (b) State one way in which today's coins resemble the ancient ones in what they are made of, and one way in which they differ.
questions.a: (a) An alloy is a metal made by combining two or more metallic elements, and this makes the coin strong. (b) Both are alloys; the ancient alloys were of silver and copper, whereas today's coins are alloys consisting largely of iron with chromium, silicon and carbon.
s: Part (a): an alloy combines metals and makes the coin strong
Part (b): both are alloys, but the ancient ones were silver and copper while today's are largely iron

questions.q:
The Arthashastra says: 'An annual salary of 60 panas could be substituted by an adhaka of grain per day, enough for four meals.' One adhaka is about 3 kg. The same book fixes the fine for failing to help a neighbour at 100 panas. Take a year as 365 days.
(a) How many kilograms of grain does one adhaka a day give in a year?
(b) So, to the nearest kilogram, how much grain was one pana worth?
(c) How many times the annual salary of 60 panas was the fine?
(d) One reader says the fine was meant to raise money for the ruler. Another says it was meant to make people value helping neighbours. Which reading do your figures support better? Name one further piece of evidence that would help.
questions.a: (a) 365 x 3 = 1,095 kg. (b) 1,095 / 60 = 18.25, about 18 kg. (c) 100 / 60, about 1.7 times. (d) The fine was larger than a whole year's salary, which fits the idea that helping a neighbour was valued; to be sure, one would want to know whether the fines were actually collected or what the ruler did with them.
s: Part (a): 1,095 kg
Part (b): about 18 kg
Part (c): about 1.7 times
Part (d): a reading supported by the figures plus one useful extra evidence

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the idea of the chapter it illustrates in Column B.
Column A: 1. A merchant from a small kingdom finds a large kingdom's coins accepted in his market.  2. Archaeologists find Roman gold coins in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.  3. A Kannada-speaking shopkeeper calls money 'haNa'.  4. A coin issued in 2021 marks 75 years of independence.
Column B: a. Coins of powerful rulers were accepted across various kingdoms.  b. Southern India traded with the rest of the world by sea.  c. A form of the ancient word 'pana' survives in a language today.  d. Special coins are minted to mark important events for the nation.
questions.a: A large kingdom's coins accepted elsewhere show acceptance across kingdoms; Roman coins in Kerala and Tamil Nadu show maritime trade; 'haNa' is a form of the ancient pana; the 2021 coin is a special coin for a national event. Each wrong pairing swaps two of these.

questions.q: A student writes: 'The ₹ sign was designed by a committee of the Reserve Bank of India and adopted in 1947.' Correct the two errors using the chapter.
questions.a: The sign was adopted by the Government of India in 2010, not 1947, and it was designed by Udaya Kumar from the Indian Institute of Technology, Bombay (Mumbai), not by a committee of the Reserve Bank of India.
s: Year corrected to 2010, adopted by the Government of India
Designer corrected to Udaya Kumar of IIT Bombay

questions.q: Excavations in a market town yield 15 coins issued by its own ruler and 85 coins issued by a distant powerful ruler. Which inference fits the chapter's account?
questions.a: The chapter says rulers controlled the minting of their coins, and that the coins of powerful rulers came to be accepted across various kingdoms, not just their own. So the 85 coins show the distant ruler's coins were accepted in this market. They do not prove he ruled the town.
o: The distant ruler's coins were accepted in this market, helping trade across geographies
The town must have been ruled by the distant ruler, since his coins outnumber the local ones
The town's own ruler did not control the minting of coins, as his coins are fewer in number
The town carried on only barter, because the coins were never used to buy anything there

questions.q: Write three clues for a class quiz whose answer is 'karshapana'. Each clue must use a fact from the chapter and the three together should point only to this answer.
questions.a: Examples: it was an ancient Indian coin; it was made of gold, silver, copper or their alloys; it is also called a pana and carried symbols called rupas; it was issued by rulers.
s: Clue 1 is correct and from the chapter
Clue 2 is correct and different from clue 1
Clues together point only to the karshapana

questions.q: (a) What were the symbols punched on ancient coins called, and what were the coins themselves called? (b) Which words for money in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam and Kannada are forms of one of these names, and in which languages is each used?
questions.a: (a) The symbols were called rupas and the coins were called karshapanas or panas. (b) The word is a form of pana: panam in Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam, and hana in Kannada.
s: Part (a): rupas for the symbols; karshapanas or panas for the coins
Part (b): panam in Tamil, Telugu and Malayalam; hana in Kannada

questions.q: A student describes an ancient Indian coin: 'It is a piece of pure gold, minted by any trader who wanted to, with plain surfaces and no marks, and it could be used only in the kingdom that made it.' Rewrite the description to match the chapter by correcting each of the four errors, and add the names by which such coins were known.
questions.a: Such coins were made from precious metals like gold, silver and copper or their alloys, not pure gold alone. Their minting and issue were controlled entirely by rulers, not by any trader. They carried symbols punched on them called rupas, and their two sides, the obverse and reverse, bore motifs such as animals, trees, hills, kings or queens and deities. The coins of powerful rulers came to be accepted across various kingdoms, which helped trade. They were called karshapanas or panas.
s: Corrects the metal: gold, silver, copper or their alloys
Corrects the issuer: controlled entirely by rulers
Corrects the plain surfaces: symbols called rupas and motifs on the two sides
Corrects the use: powerful rulers' coins accepted across kingdoms, helping trade
Gives the names karshapanas or panas

questions.q: A student designs a new symbol for a currency: a Roman letter 'R' with a single stripe below it, and says it follows the chapter's ₹ sign. Which statement about her design is correct?
questions.a: The chapter says the ₹ sign mixes the Devanagari 'Ra' and the Roman 'R', with two parallel horizontal stripes running at the top that stand for the national flag and the 'equal to' sign. Her design has no Devanagari 'Ra' and only one stripe, placed below.
o: It leaves out the Devanagari 'Ra' and has one stripe below, not two parallel stripes at the top
It matches the ₹ sign, which is a Roman 'R' with a single stripe below it
It leaves out only the Devanagari 'Ra'; the ₹ sign also has a single stripe below the letter
It matches the ₹ sign except that the ₹ sign was first designed in the year 1947

questions.q: A quarter-anna coin is worth one-fourth of an anna. Using the chapter's value of an anna, (a) how many quarter-anna coins make one anna, and (b) how many quarter-anna coins make one rupee?
questions.a: (a) 4 quarter-anna coins make one anna. (b) One anna is 1/16 of a rupee, so a rupee is 16 annas, and 16 x 4 = 64 quarter-anna coins.
s: Part (a): 4 quarter-anna coins to the anna
Part (b): 16 annas to the rupee, so 64 quarter-anna coins

questions.q: Imran says, 'In 1947 a one-rupee coin could buy exactly 10 dozen bananas.' Using the chapter's facts that one anna was 1/16 of a rupee and bought a dozen bananas, show that Imran is wrong.
questions.a: One rupee is 16 annas, and each anna bought a dozen bananas, so a rupee bought 16 dozen, which is 192 bananas. 10 dozen is only 120 bananas, so Imran is wrong.
s: Converts one rupee to 16 annas
Finds 16 dozen or 192 bananas
Compares it with 10 dozen or 120 and states the claim is wrong

questions.q:
A group of students collected old coins as a class activity: 3 half-anna coins (1942), 2 quarter-anna coins (1918) and 2 one-anna coins (1943). A quarter-anna is one-fourth of an anna and a half-anna is half of an anna. Their teacher also lends them a coin issued in 2021 to mark 75 years of independence.
(a) What is the total value of the old collection in annas?
(b) What fraction of a rupee is that?
(c) How many bananas could that total have bought in 1947?
(d) They may display only one coin at the front: the 1918 quarter-anna or the 2021 coin. Which shows more about how money in India has changed? Justify using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 3 x 1/2 + 2 x 1/4 + 2 x 1 = 4 annas. (b) 4/16 = 1/4 of a rupee. (c) 4 annas = 4 dozen = 48 bananas. (d) Either coin is acceptable with a reason: the 1918 coin shows an old denomination (the anna) that is now gone; the 2021 coin shows that special coins are still minted to mark national events.
s: Part (a): 4 annas
Part (b): 1/4 of a rupee
Part (c): 48 bananas
Part (d): a choice justified with the chapter's coin facts

questions.q: Explain how coins helped trade in ancient India, using the coins of powerful rulers and the Roman coins found in Pudukkottai. Then suggest two steps that rulers might have taken so that their coins were accepted in other kingdoms or countries, giving a reason for each.
questions.a: The coins of powerful rulers were accepted across kingdoms and not just their own, which boosted trade across geographies. Roman gold coins found in Pudukkottai and parts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu show maritime trade with the world, and scholars conclude the trade was in favour of India. Possible steps with reasons: keep a fixed metal quality, so that traders trust the coin; use a well-known symbol, so that it is recognised; make trade agreements with other rulers.
s: Powerful rulers' coins accepted across kingdoms to help trade
Roman coins as evidence of maritime trade in Kerala and Tamil Nadu
Scholars' conclusion that trade favoured India
First suggested step with a reason
Second suggested step with a reason
